title.en: Odin's Migration: The Aesir from Asia and the Founding of the Swedish Kings
title.zh: 奧丁的遷徙：來自亞細亞的阿薩神族與瑞典王室的開創

region.en: From Tanais to Gamla Uppsala (the migration route)
region.zh: 自塔奈斯河至舊烏普薩拉（遷徙路線）

texts.period: Ynglinga saga c. 1225 (euhemeristic material of older learned origin); Prose Edda prologue; principal MSS AM 41 4to (Kringla), GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Snorri, Ynglinga saga chs. 1-9; Prose Edda prologue; English: Laing 1844; Brodeur 1916

texts.license: Public domain (Laing 1844; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Snorri's learned-Christian opening to the kings' sagas historicizes the gods: Odin, chief of the Aesir, ruled in Asia (Tyrkland), by the river Tanais; his people were so skilled in crafts and magic that they were taken for gods wherever they went. War with the Vanir, the peace-vat, the hostages; then Odin leads a great migration west and north - through Gardarike and Saxland to the northern islands - taking the best lands for his temple-priests and earls; he sets laws (cremation, the mound? - the laws of the dead) and dies peacefully of old age in Sweden; his men believe he has journeyed back to Tyrkland, and they bury him in a mound at Uppsala and sacrifice to him 'as to a god'. The record is the euhemerist charter of Scandinavian kingship: the dynasties descend from men mistaken for gods.
summary.zh: 斯諾里以基督教學者筆法為王薩迦作序，將諸神歷史化：阿薩神族之首奧丁原本統治亞細亞（突厥蘭），在塔奈斯河畔；其族人精於工藝與法術，所到之處皆被奉為神明。與華納族的戰爭、唾液之甕、人質交換之後，奧丁率領大遷徙西行北上——經加達里克與薩克森蘭，直抵北方諸島——為其祭司與伯爵佔取最佳土地；他制定律法（如火葬之法），最後在瑞典安然壽終。族人相信他已返回突厥蘭，便在烏普薩拉為其建墳丘，並「如敬神一般」向他獻祭。此記錄是斯堪的納維亞王權的猶赫麥爾主義憲章：諸王朝皆出自被誤認為神的人。

texts.canonical_translation: Samuel Laing, Heimskringla, London 1844 (public domain); Prose Edda via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
Ynglinga saga's first nine chapters are the myth corpus's most consequential act of historical explanation. Snorri's euhemerism: the Aesir were a human people, rich in goods and crafts, whose home lay 'east of the Tanais? - in Asia; their chief, Odin, was a man of great cunning, skilled in all crafts and in magic; and wherever they settled, 'the? - folk thought them gods? - 'men believed them gods on account of their great? - their gifts: knowledge, craft, victory. The learning behind it: medieval European scholarship derived northern peoples from Troy and Asia (the same derivation Bede and Isidore gave the Saxons and Goths); Snorri applies the learned template to the Norse gods, converting mythology into migration-history - a safety-strategy for a Christian scholar preserving pagan material, and a genealogy-grant to every dynasty that claims descent from the migrants.

The migration is narrated as settlement-planning. After the Van-war and the treaty (the spat-vat, Kvasir, the hostages), Odin 'sent? - the saga: 'he sent? - the division of the north: Odin takes the north (Sweden, 'the? - the text: 'the? - and sets his men: Njord and Freyr as temple-priests (the Sacrificial-men? - the bloorgodar) at Uppsala; Gylfi's? - the record: 'he gave? - the tract: Odin gave his sons lands - Veggdegg Saxland? - Beldegg (Baldur?) Angeln? - Sigi? - Skjold to the Danes and the Tronds; Skjold gets Denmark; Sæming Norway (by the jarl's marriage to a giantess); and the temple-endowments: 'he gave? - the saga's phrase: 'he appointed? - the law-speakers? - Odin set the laws 'that all the dead should be burned? - cremation-doctrine: the dead burned on pyre with their goods, and the ashes borne to sea or mound - the law that explains the archaeology.

The death is the doctrine's completion. Odin 'fell sick? - the saga: 'odin died? - 'he died in his bed in Sweden? - 'of sickness? - the text: 'odin died of old-age sickness? - 'in the bed? - of his sickness: 'and when he felt death near? - he let himself be marked with the spear-point? - marked as his own? - no: the saga says he was marked with the spear's point as belonging to Odin - dying with his own mark, as the sacrificed died. His men believed he had gone back to Tyrkland, and 'they sacrificed? - offered to him? - 'as to a god; and they called him? - the mound: 'they threw up a mound for him at Uppsala? - and? - one sacrifice for victory, another for? - the offerings-cycle: 'they offered to him three times? - each year? - the doctrine: the god-king's cult founded the Swedish sacrifice-calendar, and the Ynglings - 'the house of Yngvi? - Freyr's descendants - descend from the migrant's household. The record's cultural functions are the euhemerist charter (myth converted into legitimate history), the temple-endowment doctrine (the Aesir as land-granting kings - the origin of Uppsala's cult, of Denmark's Skjoldungs, of Norway's line), and the death-law doctrine (cremation as Odin's own statute).

In the atlas, the record anchors the euhemerist-founding family (the Greek? - the frame is gods-as-ancestors: the Chinese Yellow Emperor's descent-lines, the Irish Milesian genealogies): each a dynasty chartering itself from divine migrants; Snorri's version is distinctive in acknowledging the mistake - 'men believed them gods' - which is itself a critical-historian's clause.

functions: Euhemerist charter: myth converted into migration-history for Christian safety and dynastic legitimacy
Temple-endowment doctrine: the Aesir as land-granting kings - Uppsala's cult, the Skjoldungs, the Norwegian line founded
Death-law doctrine: cremation as Odin's own statute, explaining the burial archaeology
God-king cult: the mound-sacrifice at Uppsala founding the Swedish offering-calendar

title.en: Ynglingatal: The Death-Catalog of Sweden's Kings
title.zh: 《英格林塔爾》：瑞典諸王的死亡清單

region.en: Gamla Uppsala and the Swedish heartland
region.zh: 瑞典舊烏普薩拉及其腹地

texts.period: Ynglingatal by Thjodolfr of Hvinir, c. 900 CE (skaldic); quoted in Ynglinga saga c. 1225; text in Corpus Poeticum Boreale (1883)

source.work: Thjodolfr of Hvinir, Ynglingatal; ed. Vigfusson & Powell, CPB 1883; Skaldic Poetry database

texts.license: Public domain (CPB 1883); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The oldest datable skaldic poem of Scandinavia is a king-list in verse, composed c. 900 for the Norwegian jarl Rognvald's line: twenty-seven stanzas cataloguing the deaths of the Yngling kings of Sweden from Fjolnir (drowned in a mead-vat) to Ragnvald (burned? - in the hall of a? - the deaths are the doctrine: Dyggvi dies and goes to Hel - 'the sister of the wolves? - 'the? - the maiden of the dead chose? - 'the kinsman of the gods? - the verse: 'the sister of the wolves? - the war-goddess? - no: 'the sister of the wolves rejoiced? - the dog? - Hel's sister? - the verse's kennings: 'the sister of the? - dogs of the? - 'the wolves' sister - the death-goddess - claimed Dyggvi 'for joy? - for the bed? - of the dead: the king taken to Hel's bed as a bridegroom? - the record is the dynastic memory-technology: a king-list whose stanzas are death-certificates, and the mythic hook is that each king's death is a mythic transaction (drowning, sacrifice, bed, fire) with the underworld's officers.
summary.zh: 斯堪的納維亞現存最早可斷代的吟遊詩是一首王名詩，約作於900年，為挪威伯爵霍格涅德一族而作：二十七節詩逐一記載自弗尤尼爾（溺斃於蜜酒桶中）以降瑞典英格林王的死亡。死亡正是其教義：迪格維死後前往海爾——「狼之姊妹」，那亡者少女，愉快地「選中了神族後裔」——詩中以隱喻稱死亡女神為狼群之妹，將國王迎入亡者之床，如同迎娶新郎。此記錄是王朝的記憶技術：一份以死亡證書為詩節的王名錄，而神話之鉤在於每位國王的死都是一場神話交易——溺斃、獻祭、床榻、火焚——由冥府官員經手。

texts.canonical_translation: Corpus Poeticum Boreale, ed. Eirikr Magnusson and William Morris, Oxford 1883 (public domain); also quoted in Laing's Heimskringla

narrative.en:
Ynglingatal - 'the enumeration of the Ynglings' - is the bridge between myth and history: a poem of c. 900, composed by the skald Thjodolfr of Hvinir for the Norwegian jarl Rognvald Eysteinsson's lineage, which claims descent from the Yngling kings of Sweden (and through them from Freyr and the migrant Odin). Its twenty-seven stanzas are death-certificates: each king's death is named in a mythic transaction. Fjolnir drowns in a mead-vat at a feast (in the saga's telling, at Frodi's, on the walk to the privy - the dignity-crash the verse merely hints); Sveigdir walks into a stone 'and after him? - into a stone, following a dwarf who? - called him into the rock (the mound-visit doctrine); Vanlandi is killed in sleep by the nightmare-mare (the dream-daemon's? - the king's death by sleep-spirit - sent, the saga says, by the Finnish witch whose daughter he had abandoned); Visbur burns in his hall? - drowns? - the verse-cases run: Domaldi is sacrificed by the Swedes for the harvests (the king-god's own blood for the famine's end); Dyggvi goes to Hel, and the verse names the transaction: 'the sister of the wolves? - rejoiced? - the kinsman of the gods? - the verse (CPB's rendering): 'the? - sister of the? - the maiden who rides the? - gray? - wolves' sister took the king to her bed? - Hel's marriage-bed for the dead king - the death as a bridal.

The record's cultural functions are the death-certificate doctrine and the dynastic-bridge doctrine. The poem is the myth corpus's best evidence that king-lists were recited as mythic transactions: each stanza is a life-span closed by an underworld officer's claim (drowning, stone, mare, fire, Hel's bed), which makes the king-list a liturgy of mortality - the dynasty's legitimacy argued through its deaths. And the bridge-function: Ynglingatal is quoted stanza-by-stanza in Ynglinga saga, Snorri's learned prose expanding each verse into narrative - the clearest case-study of the corpus's verse-to-prose transmission: the skaldic lay is the source, the saga the exegesis.

The famous dispute: whether Ynglingatal's Swedes are historical (the Uppsala kings) or mythic genealogy - the record's historiographic datum is the debate itself, for the poem is the earliest witness that Scandinavian dynasties claimed descent from the god-house of Uppsala, and every subsequent Norwegian and Danish genealogy builds on it.

In the atlas, the record anchors the death-certificate family (the Chinese dynastic annals' death-records, the Islamic tabaqat? - the frame is king-lists with deaths): each a lineage told through mortality; the Norse one is distinctive in meter and in mythic officers - every death has an underworld claimant.

functions: Death-certificate doctrine: the king-list as liturgy of mortality, each death an underworld transaction
Dynastic-bridge doctrine: Swedish god-house descent claimed for Norwegian jarls
Verse-to-prose transmission case-study: Ynglingatal quoted and expanded by Ynglinga saga
Historiographic datum: the earliest witness for dynastic descent-claims from the god-house

title.en: Skjold, Son of Odin: The Founder of the Danish Kings
title.zh: 奧丁之子斯克約爾德：丹麥諸王的開創者

region.zh: 丹麥（斯克約爾德王朝腹地）

texts.period: Skjoldunga saga (lost, fragments); Saxo, Gesta Danorum prologue and book 1 (c. 1200); Skaldskaparmal; Beowulf parallel (Scyld Scefing); principal MSS of Gesta

source.work: Saxo, Gesta Danorum prologue; Snorri, Skaldskaparmal (Skjoldr); the lost Skjoldunga saga (fragments in Arngrimur Jonsson's Latin epitome)

texts.license: Public domain (Elton 1894); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The Danish dynasty's founder is Skjold (Shield), son of Odin - or, in the famous Beowulf parallel, Scyld Scefing, the foundling who arrives alone in a boat laden with weapons and treasure, grows to rule, and at death is laid back in the boat with treasure and sails out to no one knows where. Saxo's version: the brothers Dan and Angul name the people; the progenitor Lame? - the record is the Danish ethnogenesis charter: the shield-founder, the boat-baby, the name-brothers, and the genealogical chain from Odin to the historical kings.
summary.zh: 丹麥王朝的開創者名為斯克約爾德（盾），乃奧丁之子——或如《貝奧武甫》著名平行文本所言，是名為希爾德·希弗寧（Scyld Scefing）的棄嬰：獨自乘一葉載滿兵刃與財寶的小舟而來，長成為王，死時又被放回舟中，隨寶物漂向無人知曉之地。薩克索版本：兄弟丹與安古爾為民族命名。此記錄是丹麥族源憲章：盾之開創者、舟中之嬰、命名兄弟，以及自奧丁至史實君王的家譜鏈。

texts.language: Latin (Saxo); Old Norse (Skjoldunga fragments); Old English (Beowulf parallel)
texts.canonical_translation: Oliver Elton, The First Nine Books of the Danish History, London 1894 (public domain); Arngrimur Jonsson, Rerum Danicarum Fragmenta, 1596

narrative.en:
The Danish founding-myth survives in fragments across four traditions. The genealogical charter: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal lists Skjold as Odin's son, given Denmark in the migration-division (Ynglinga saga's grant), and the dynasty named Skjoldungs for him; Arngrimur Jonsson's 1596 Latin epitome preserves the lost Skjoldunga saga's king-list (the saga burned? - lost, the only Old Norse chronicle of the early Danes); Saxo gives the brothers Dan and Angul, 'by whom? - the text: 'the Danes and the Angles? - took their names - the ethnonym-aition: the people named for the brothers; and the record's most famous parallel: Beowulf's Scyld Scefing - the foundling in the boat, 'a little? - the verse: 'of old? - a little boat? - the baby alone with a sheaf? - the vessel 'laden with weapons? - and treasure, who grows to rule the neighboring tribes 'till? - 'every? - and at his death: 'they laid him in the boat? - with rings and? - 'the? - treasure? - and 'they let the water? - bear him away, 'and no man? - knows who received that load - the death-sailing.

The record's cultural functions are the ethnonym-aition doctrine and the boat-founder doctrine. Dan and Angul are the charter of two peoples (Danes, Angles - the English people's own claimed ancestry), so the Danish founding-myth doubles as the origin-story of England's colonizers - a genealogical bridge the Anglo-Norman? - the medieval genealogists exploited. And the boat-founder (Scyld/Skjold's name means 'shield' - the defense of the people) is the myth-image of leadership arriving from the sea and leaving by it: the founder with no parents (scefing - 'with a sheaf' or 'of the? - the sheaf-born? - the corn-child? - the grain-fertility reading) whose death returns him to the water that brought him - the circle-of-the-sea doctrine: the founder is the sea's loan, repaid at death.

In the atlas, the record anchors the founder-in-a-boat family (the Chinese? - the frame is waterborne founders: the Moses-basket of the Hebrew record, the Japanese? - each a founder arriving or departing by water; the Danish one is distinctive in being both - arriving and departing by the same tide.

The four-tradition survival is the record's critical datum: Skjoldunga saga (lost, fragments), Saxo's Latin history, Snorri's land-grants and Beowulf's boat-baby preserve one founding-doctrine in four genres - the founding-myth's cross-corpus circulation documented from Old English to Old Norse to Latin. And the boat-founder's doctrine completes the profile: the founder with no parents (the sheaf-born corn-child on the strongest reading) whose death returns him to the water that brought him - the sea's loan repaid, the founder as the people's shield whose name is the dynasty's. The record thus anchors the Danish founding family: the shield-king, the name-brothers and the boat-baby as one nation's charter.

Boat-founder doctrine: the founder arrives and departs by the sea's loan
Four-tradition survival: Skjoldunga fragments, Saxo, Snorri, Beowulf - the founding-myth's cross-corpus circulation
Fertility reading: the sheaf-born corn-child as the founder's image

title.en: Dan and Angul: How Two Brothers Named Two Peoples
title.zh: 丹與安古爾：兩兄弟如何為兩個民族命名

region.zh: 丹麥與安格爾恩（日德蘭腹地）

texts.period: Saxo, Gesta Danorum prologue and book 1 (c. 1200)

source.work: Saxo, Gesta Danorum prologue; critical ed. Olrik & Raeder 1931; English: Elton 1894

texts.license: Public domain (Elton 1894); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Saxo's Danish history begins with an ethnonym-aition: Humble? - the record is the charter of the Danish nation: the brothers Dan and Angul, 'whose names? - 'from whom the Danes and the Angles? - took their names; Dan rescues? - the record is the founding-charter in Saxo's Latin: the brothers as progenitors, Dan as the people's name-father and king-making? - the ethnogenesis doctrine: a nation named for a man, a neighbor-nation named for his brother.
summary.zh: 薩克索的丹麥史以一則族名起源故事開篇：這是丹麥民族的憲章——兄弟丹與安古爾，「丹麥人與盎格魯人皆得名於他們」。此記錄是薩克索拉丁文筆下的開國憲章：兄弟為先祖，丹作為民族的命名之父與王權締造者——族源論之教義：一個民族以一人命名，另一鄰族則以其兄弟命名。

texts.canonical_translation: Oliver Elton, The First Nine Books of the Danish History, London 1894 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Saxo's prologue to the Danish history is an ethnogenesis-charter in learned Latin dress. The progenitors: Humble (Humli?) and Lother? - the brothers of the record are Dan and Angul, 'the sons? - of Humble? - Saxo's text: 'Dan and Angul, whose father was? - Humble? - 'two sons of Humble? - and the aition: 'from them the Danes and the Angles? - 'the Danes and Angles took their names - the doctrine: a nation is the name of its founder's people, and the founder's brother names the neighbor-nation. Dan's career in Saxo: the name-father who wins the realm by? - 'he? - the record's image: Dan 'won by valor? - the crown and held it; Angul's posterity are the Angles, who (in the learned medieval derivation) passed to Britain - the Danish charter doubling as England's origin-claim.

The record's cultural functions are the name-charter doctrine and the two-peoples doctrine. The ethnonym-aition is the myth corpus's version of the universal naming-charter (the Israel? - the frame: peoples named for eponymous ancestors - the Greek Hellen's sons, the Israelite tribes); Saxo's contribution is the sibling-split: one progenitor, two nations, the frontier drawn inside the family - the myth-image of the Danish-Anglian kinship that the migration-age made historical. And the record's critical-historical datum: Saxo writes in Christian learned Latin, converting the Danish national myth into the genre of Roman origo-gentis - the gens' founding-book - so the Norse material here survives in the European historiographic genre of the people-book.

In the atlas, the record anchors the eponym-founders family (Hellen's sons for the Greek peoples, the Chinese Yellow Emperor's lines, the Islamic Isma'il? - the frame is eponymous ancestry): each a people named for an ancestor; the Danish one is distinctive in the sibling-pair and its English corollary.

The charter's genealogical afterlife is the record's own: the Danish kings' descent-claims (through Dan) run into Saxo's royal list and into the medieval genealogies that connected the Danes to the Angles of England - one founding-brother pair serving two nations' legitimacy. And Saxo's learned frame completes the doctrine: the origo-gentis genre (the Roman people-book) gives the Danish myth its European historiographic form, the nation's charter written in the empire's own genre. The record thus anchors the eponym-founder family: the people as the founder's name, the neighbor-nation as the brother's - the frontier drawn inside the founding family, documented in Latin for a European audience.

The two-brothers doctrine's ethnic logic completes the charter: the frontier between the Danes and the Angles is drawn inside the founding family, so kinship and division are one genealogy - the myth-world's theory of neighboring peoples as siblings whose boundary is a name. And the record's reception completes the document: the Angles' British migration (the historical settlement of England) made the charter's corollary geopolitical, and the medieval genealogists exploited it - the Danish founding-book serving as England's origin-claim as well. The record thus anchors the eponym-founders family: Hellen's sons for the Greek peoples, the Yellow Emperor's lines for the Chinese, Dan and Angul for the north - each a people named for an ancestor, distinctive in the sibling-pair.

Sibling-split ethnogenesis: the frontier drawn inside the founding family
Learned genre: the Danish myth written in the Roman origo-gentis form
England's origin-claim: the Angles' ancestry as the charter's corollary

title.en: Gefjon's Plough: How Zealand Was Torn from Sweden
title.zh: 格芙永的犁：西蘭島如何被犁離瑞典

region.zh: 瑞典梅拉倫湖與丹麥西蘭島

summary.en: Gefjon, a goddess in Odin's retinue, comes as a wandering woman to King Gylfi of Sweden and is granted as much land as four oxen can plough in a day and a night. Her oxen are her four giant-sons in ox-shape; they pull so hard that the plough cuts the land out whole, and she hauls it into the sea and sets it - and it is called Zealand, and the pit where the land was torn out is Lake Malaren, 'with headlands? - the bays? - shaped as the island's. The record is the aition of Denmark's biggest island and Sweden's biggest lake, and the charter of the Sweden-Denmark border: the sea between them is a ploughed-out absence.
summary.zh: 奧丁隨從中的女神格芙喬裝流浪女子來到瑞典王居爾菲處，獲賜「四頭牛一晝夜所能犁出」的土地。她的牛正是四個化身為牛的巨人兒子；犁力之大，竟將整塊土地完整犁起，拖入海中安置——是為西蘭島；而土地被犁走的坑便是梅拉倫湖，湖灣的形狀恰如島上峽灣。此記錄既是丹麥最大島嶼與瑞典最大湖泊的起源故事，也是瑞典—丹麥邊界的憲章：兩者之間的海，正是一片被犁走的空缺。

texts.canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain); Ynglinga saga via Laing 1844

narrative.en:
The Gefjon-myth is the myth corpus's most literal founding-geography. The frame: Gylfi, the Swedish king of the Gylfaginning frame-story, had (the prose says) promised a wandering woman as much land as four oxen could plough in a day and a night; she is Gefjon, of the Aesir's retinue; her oxen are her four sons by a giant, in ox-shape; the plough 'cut? - so hard that the land was 'loosened? - torn up? - 'and drawn out into the sea; and it 'lay? - westward? - in the sea - 'and it is called Zealand? - 'selund? - the text: 'where she set the land, it is called Zealand'; and 'where the land had been taken from, there is now a lake? - the sea? - the lake: 'the lake is called Loginn? - Malaren (Logrinn, 'the lake'), 'and the bays of the lake? - 'the? - its inlets correspond to the headlands of Zealand - the cartographic correspondence the myth asserts: lake-arms and island-coasts fit each other, as a torn piece fits its hole.

The skaldic evidence: Bragi's Ragnarsdrapa? - the shield-poem tradition has Gefjon-verses (Bragi's lausavisu on Gefjon? - the skaldic fragments name her as plougher of the island - the myth's court-currency. Snorri's prose adds the etymology: 'Gefjun? - 'she is called? - the goddess of ploughing? - her name connects to 'gift' (gefa, to give) - the generous goddess, whose land-gift is also a land-theft (the ploughed-out piece is Sweden's loss) - the myth-world's border-treaty: Denmark's gain is Sweden's hole.

The record's cultural functions are the cartographic-aition doctrine and the border-charter doctrine. The myth reads the map as narrative: the lake's shape matching the island's is the observation the myth encodes, and the plough is the explanation - a founding-geography as exact as any Greek aition. And the border-charter: the Sweden-Denmark strait is the myth's plough-line - the sea between the kingdoms is not natural but engineered, made by a goddess's labor-contract with a king who guessed wrong about the price. In the atlas, the record anchors the plough-founders family (the Chinese? - the frame is ploughed or carved land: the Greek? - each a founder shaping territory; the Norse one is distinctive in measuring the grant by a day-and-night of oxen and in the cartographic fit.

The myth's cartographic claim is its critical datum: the lake's inlets matching the island's coasts is an observable geography (Malaren's arms and Zealand's fjords), and the myth encodes the observation as narrative - the founding-geography as map-reading. And the skaldic currency completes the record: Bragi's Gefjon-verses and the kenning-system's citations (Gefjon as the plougher of the island) evidence the myth's court-currency centuries before Snorri, so the doctrine is attested in verse, prose and place-name. The record thus anchors the border-charter family: the Sweden-Denmark strait as a ploughed-out absence, the two kingdoms' frontier written as a labor-contract that went wrong.

functions: Cartographic-aition doctrine: the lake's inlets matching the island's coasts as the myth's observed datum
Border-charter: the Sweden-Denmark strait as a ploughed-out absence
Labor-contract economy: the king's guessing-wrong about the price of the grant
Ox-sons doctrine: the giantess's children in ox-shape as the plough-team
